Drawing on data from the full Tribunal record, Air Canada’s responses and a content analysis of 47 news articles, the study traces a three-phase crisis lifecycle and identifies a mismatch between Air Canada’s deflection-based response and the rebuild suggestion of the Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) for high attribution crises.
one_line_summary: Analyzes Air Canada's AI chatbot liability case to refine crisis communication theory for AI-mediated accountability.
annotation: This study examines the Moffatt v. Air Canada tribunal ruling—the first Canadian case assigning organizational liability for misleading AI chatbot outputs—to analyze how existing crisis communication frameworks inadequately address AI-mediated accountability. Using tribunal records, organizational responses, and content analysis of news coverage, the paper traces a three-phase crisis lifecycle and critiques Air Canada's deflection strategy against Situational Crisis Communication Theory recommendations. The paper does not build or apply AI/ML models but critically examines the governance, legal, and communicative implications of deploying AI in customer-facing roles.

title: Trusted Execution Environments in Systems-of-Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study
abstract: Security in Systems-of-Systems remains a major challenge due to their distributed, heterogeneous, and autonomous nature. Trusted Execution Environments have emerged as a promising hardware-based approach to address confidentiality, integrity, and trust in such complex ecosystems. However, the application of TEE within SoS lacks a systematic overview. This study conducts a Systematic Mapping Study to comprehensively assess the current state of TEE adoption in SoS, identifying primary challenges, outcomes, and evaluation approaches. A reproducible protocol was applied across four scientific databases, yielding 301 studies, of which 39 were selected for detailed analysis. Findings reveal that research predominantly addresses domains such as Smart Grids, Industrial IoT, and Smart Cities, focusing on requirements such as confidentiality, attestation, privacy, and isolation. Key challenges include performance overhead, hardware-level vulnerabilities, and integration complexity. Despite these obstacles, TEE technologies demonstrate transformative potential by enabling new architectural patterns for secure computation, privacy-preserving collaboration, and trustworthy system integration. The study also highlights underexplored application areas and proposes a research agenda that emphasizes lightweight TEE, interoperability, and robust evaluation methodologies. Finally, this SMS identifies research gaps and proposes future directions to expand TEE adoption and improve scalability, interoperability, and empirical validation in SoS environments.
one_line_summary: Systematic mapping study of Trusted Execution Environments adoption in Systems-of-Systems security contexts.
annotation: This paper conducts a systematic mapping study of Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) adoption across Systems-of-Systems domains such as Smart Grids, Industrial IoT, and Smart Cities, focusing on security challenges related to confidentiality, integrity, and trust. While the primary contribution is a security architecture survey rather than an AI/ML contribution, TEEs are increasingly relevant to AI deployment contexts, particularly for securing federated learning and confidential AI inference workloads. The AI relevance is peripheral, as the paper does not build or evaluate AI models but surveys hardware-based security infrastructure that intersects with AI system deployment.

title: Cyberbullying Safety Engineering by Patent: Trends, Solution Paradigms, and Societal Impacts
abstract: Cyberbullying is a socio-technical safety challenge, and industry priorities are most clearly revealed in the inventions it patents. Treating patents as forward-looking proxies of engineering attention, we analyze 192 patent families (1983–mid-2025) using a mixed-methods approach that combines descriptive analytics, dual-coded thematic analysis, and LDA/BERTopic to map eight solution paradigms and their intended beneficiaries. We observe a sharp increase in filings from the mid-2010s, dominated by AI-centric detection and moderation pipelines, with comparatively little attention to reporting, privacy, or ethics. Only 9.4% of patent families explicitly reference minors, while other high-risk groups are largely absent, reflecting uneven beneficiary coverage. This landscape provides a novel lens on who is protected, how, and by which mechanisms, and offers actionable insights for software engineering practice, education, and policy. We further translate these findings into equity-focused requirements that highlight opportunities for more accountable and inclusive cyberbullying interventions.
one_line_summary: Patent analysis of cyberbullying safety engineering reveals AI-dominated detection trends and uneven beneficiary coverage.
annotation: This paper analyzes 192 cyberbullying-related patent families using descriptive analytics, thematic coding, and topic modeling (LDA/BERTopic) to map solution paradigms in the patent landscape. While AI/ML methods are used as analytical tools and AI-centric detection pipelines are a major subject of the patents examined, the paper's core contribution is a sociotechnical critique of industry priorities in cyberbullying safety engineering rather than the development of new AI systems. The findings highlight that AI-dominated moderation solutions receive disproportionate patent attention while ethical, privacy, and vulnerable-population considerations remain underrepresented.

title: The Cognitive Obesity Hypothesis: AI and the Risk of Mental Atrophy
abstract: For two centuries, the mechanization of physical labor delivered enormous gains in productivity and comfort while quietly eroding the bodies it served. Adults in wealthy countries now grip with roughly 20% less force than their counterparts did in the mid-1980s, expend on the order of 100--140 fewer occupational kilocalories per day than in the 1960s, and live in environments where physical inactivity is implicated in more than five million premature deaths each year. Here, we ask whether the rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence and increasingly autonomous AI agents could be starting a structurally similar transition in the cognitive domain, and we advance this as a testable risk hypothesis rather than an established fact. Reading the physical case as a worked example, we argue that the same three-step mechanism that drove bodily decline is now plausibly acting on cognition: substitution of effort, redesign of the surrounding environment, and a rebound in which a cheaper resource is consumed in greater quantity (the Jevons paradox). We identify five early, individually preliminary signals consistent with that hypothesis: (1) reduced neural engagement during AI-assisted writing; (2) cognitive offloading and lower critical-thinking scores among adults who delegate reasoning to chatbots; (3) AI dependence associated with weaker reasoning among students; (4) deskilling in knowledge work, accelerated as passive assistants give way to agents that perform whole tasks; and (5) the displacement of the desirable difficulties known to consolidate learning. We weigh these signals against the strongest opposing case (that cognitive tools augment rather than diminish the mind) and against confounders such as the pre-existing reversal of the Flynn effect (the twentieth-century rise in measured intelligence, now declining in some cohorts for reasons unrelated to AI). Our contribution is threefold: a mechanistic parallel transferred from a fully documented, century-scale physical case; a falsifiable cellular prediction, drawn from the biology of effort, that frictionless cognitive offloading may, like disuse in muscle, produce not merely lag but measurable atrophy; and a call for the population-scale, longitudinal measurement that does not yet exist but is the precondition for testing the hypothesis before, rather than after, the fact.
one_line_summary: Hypothesizes that generative AI may cause cognitive atrophy analogous to physical decline from mechanization.
annotation: This paper advances the 'cognitive obesity hypothesis,' arguing that widespread adoption of generative AI and autonomous AI agents may erode human cognitive capacities in ways structurally analogous to how physical mechanization reduced bodily fitness over the past century. The authors draw on epidemiological and historical evidence from physical inactivity research to frame cognitive atrophy from AI reliance as a testable risk hypothesis. While the paper does not build or apply AI models, it critically examines the societal and cognitive implications of AI adoption, placing it in the peripheral relevance tier.

title: Absence of quantum advantage for approximate spin glass optimization
abstract: We perform a semiclassical, large-spin S, analysis of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, using the truncated Wigner approximation. Fixing the QAOA angles to their previously determined optimal S=1/2 values, we observe a non-monotonic dependence of the final energy on the spin. At small S the semiclassics is dominated by noise, while the large-S limit is constrained by the exponential growth of the initial fluctuations. For a depth-p QAOA one achieves the optimal balance at S of order p, resulting in a convergence of the final energy to the Parisi value like log(p)/p. We find that the semiclassics slightly outperforms the true spin-1/2 QAOA, and thus suggest they both converge to the Parisi value in the same way. Finally, removing all the initial noise, and re-optimizing the parameters to account for that change, results in superior performance with 1/p convergence.
one_line_summary: Analyzes quantum approximate optimization algorithm on spin glass models using semiclassical methods.
annotation: This paper investigates the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model, a canonical benchmark for combinatorial optimization. Using the truncated Wigner approximation for semiclassical large-spin analysis, the authors demonstrate that QAOA converges to the Parisi value at a rate of log(p)/p, suggesting no quantum advantage over classical approaches for approximate spin glass optimization. While rooted in quantum physics, the work directly evaluates the performance of a prominent quantum optimization algorithm relevant to AI and combinatorial search.

title: QMA Lower Bounds for Batch Verification via Approximate Degree
abstract: We study batch verification in QMA query and communication complexity, where the goal is to understand how the resources needed to verify $m$ copies of a Boolean function $f$ depend on $m$. We give a general technique for proving lower bounds on the witness-query tradeoff needed to batch verify a function $f$ in terms of its approximate degree. Applying this technique to an explicit family of DNF formulas $f$, we show that attempting to save even a constant factor on the witness length of the baseline approach to batch verifying $f$ necessitates a large polynomial increase in the query cost. We also obtain new lower bounds on the QMA query complexity of read-once CNF formulas and on the surjectivity and $k$-element distinctness functions. Our lower bounds also lift to give communication analogs of these results.
one_line_summary: Study of QMA query and communication complexity for batch verification using approximate degree techniques.
annotation: This paper is about quantum complexity theory (QMA complexity, query complexity, communication complexity) and is not related to AI or machine learning. While 'approximate degree' is a mathematical concept that appears in some ML theory contexts, here it is used purely in the context of quantum verification protocols and complexity lower bounds, with no connection to AI/ML systems or methods.

title: Testing Distributions Against Bounded Distinguishers
abstract: Motivated by the challenge of testing distributions over high-dimensional or continuous domains, we study distribution testing with respect to bounded classes of distinguishers. A representative task is to use samples from an unknown distribution $P$ over a very large domain to decide between two cases: $P = P_{\mathsf{ref}}$ for a fixed reference distribution $P_{\mathsf{ref}}$, or there exists a distinguisher $f$ in a bounded class $\mathcal{F}$ which witnesses the separation $|\mathbf{E}_P[f] - \mathbf{E}_{P_{\mathsf{ref}}}[f]| > ε$. This is the task of identity testing with respect to fooling distance, a name inspired by the conceptual connection with pseudorandomness. (Formally, our model instantiates integral probability metrics from Boolean classes of bounded expressivity.) We show that testing with respect to fooling distance is not only a natural computational problem that admits sample-efficient algorithms even in high-dimensional settings, but also one that reveals and underlies connections between three seemingly unrelated areas of study: testable learning, verification of learning algorithms, and testing of structured distributions (whose "$\mathcal{A}_k$-testing" model our framework extends). These connections yield new results for all of these models, including: 1. Testable proper learners using membership queries for halfspaces and decision trees. 2. A lower bound for testable PAC verification in terms of Rademacher complexity, and a distribution-free verification protocol for disjoint unions of $k$ multidimensional rectangles. 3. Identity testers (with respect to total variation distance) for decision tree distributions and distributions with low-degree polynomial densities, over Boolean and continuous hypercube domains.
one_line_summary: Studies distribution testing using bounded distinguisher classes and fooling distance metrics.
annotation: This paper investigates distribution testing (identity testing) over high-dimensional or continuous domains using integral probability metrics defined by bounded classes of distinguishers, connecting to pseudorandomness theory. The framework formalizes when an unknown distribution can be distinguished from a reference distribution by functions of bounded expressivity, which is foundational to learning theory and generative model evaluation. The work contributes theoretical results relevant to statistical learning and the evaluation of generative AI systems, where testing whether a learned distribution matches a target is a core challenge.

title: Isolation Failure From Shared Storage: Characterizing and Exploiting Page-Cache SCA Leakage Across Containers and VMs
abstract: Modern cloud platforms increasingly combine strong software isolation mechanisms with shared hardware resources to improve performance and resource efficiency. Conventional containers do this by sharing the host kernel directly, whereas sandboxed runtimes (e.g., gVisor) and VM-based runtimes (e.g., Kata, QEMU/KVM) provide progressively stronger isolation. In all cases, when tenants access host-backed filesystem state, the host page cache can remain shared and observable. Although OS-managed, this page-cache channel forms an OS-mediated microarchitectural timing side channel whose signal is shaped by the processor microarchitecture, memory and storage hierarchies, and virtualization mechanisms. We thus investigate whether unprivileged timing measurements can reveal page-cache residency across these isolation boundaries. Our evaluation covers Docker; gVisor with systrap and KVM; Kata Containers using QEMU and Cloud Hypervisor with shared host filesystems; Kata using QEMU, Cloud Hypervisor, and Firecracker with block-device-backed storage; and QEMU/KVM virtual machines under multiple host cache policies. Our results show that the timing signal persists whenever the I/O path exposes shared, host-cacheable file-backed objects, including under OverlayFS layers, virtio-fs exports, and loop-backed block devices. However, direct I/O and dedicated block devices substantially attenuate or eliminate the signal. Virtualization therefore reshapes leakage through added latency and algorithmic noise but does not remove the underlying dependence on shared hardware and cache state. We showcase this through a case study in which we recover coarse-grained activity from a WordPress deployment backed by MySQL. These results place page-cache attacks within the broader class of OS-mediated microarchitectural timing channels and motivate coordinated hardware, virtualization, and OS support for timing isolation.
one_line_summary: Investigates page-cache timing side-channel attacks across containers and VMs in cloud environments.
annotation: This paper is about microarchitectural side-channel attacks exploiting shared page-cache state across cloud isolation boundaries (containers, sandboxed runtimes, VMs). It has no meaningful connection to AI/ML methods, models, or policy.

title: Phishing and VAT Fraud in CO2 Permits: The Digital Invoice Customs Exchange Solution
abstract: In accordance with Directive 2003/87/EC of October 13, 2003, trade in greenhouse gas emissions commenced in the European Union (EU) on January 1, 2005. The EU-Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS) was born. The EU has a Value Added Tax (VAT). VAT is a transaction-based levy on all trade in goods and services. Each Member State has a VAT as a condition of membership. Until January 3, 2017 transactions in CO2 permits are taxed as services. After this date they are exempt as financial instruments. This change in VAT treatment of CO2 permits is directly attributable to rampant fraud in the market. Fraud has been so severe in CO2 permits that public trust in the EU’s emissions trading scheme has been undermined. Important lessons have been learned about controlling fraud from efforts made in the emissions markets. Unfortunately, time and political patience have run out. This paper considers a particular phishing attack in the CO2 market – the January 18, 2011 attack on the Czech registry. The focus of this paper is not on this very sensational fraud; it is on the ETS/ VAT overlap, and the ability to apply what has been learned here to the trade in gas and electricity. Careful consideration of this overlap demonstrates why the Digital Invoice Customs Exchange (DICE) proposal works as an effective fraud prevention mechanism. The moral of this story is that what we have learned can be directly applied to the commodity energy market. We know how that these markets can be secured. We need: (a) an Independent Transaction Log, and (b) a secure self-verifying digital invoice, and (c) a system of automated invoice cross-checking (the customs exchange). Can this be done? Quite simply, “yes.” A call placed to Kim Mayyasi, SmartCloud’s CEO presented this question. Not surprisingly, the response was: “… implementing a real-time transaction database of all power sales in the EU with advanced reasoning for back room analytics could implement the DICE proposal to eliminate MTIC from the EU power markets, and it could do so for the EU CO2 market right now. This is a typical challenge that our technology was designed to handle.”
one_line_summary: Examines VAT fraud and phishing in EU CO2 emissions trading and proposes digital invoice solutions.
annotation: This paper is not meaningfully related to AI or machine learning. It focuses on VAT fraud, phishing schemes, and regulatory responses within the EU Emissions Trading System, proposing a Digital Invoice Customs Exchange solution as a fraud control mechanism.

title: Offline Local Search for Online Stochastic Bandits
abstract: Combinatorial multi-armed bandits provide a fundamental online decision-making environment where a decision-maker interacts with an environment across T time steps, each time selecting an action and learning the cost of that action. The goal is to minimize regret, defined as the loss compared to the optimal fixed action in hindsight under full-information. There has been substantial interest in leveraging what is known about offline algorithm design in this online setting. Offline greedy and linear optimization algorithms (both exact and approximate) have been shown to provide useful guarantees when deployed online. We investigate local search methods, a broad class of algorithms used widely in both theory and practice, which have thus far been under-explored in this context. We focus on problems where offline local search terminates in an approximately optimal solution and give a generic method for converting such an offline algorithm into an online stochastic combinatorial bandit algorithm with O (log 3 T) (approximate) regret. In contrast, existing offline-to-online frameworks yield regret (and approximate regret) which depend sub-linearly, but polynomially on T . We demonstrate the flexibility of our framework by applying it to three online stochastic combinatorial optimization problems: scheduling to minimize total completion time, finding a minimum cost base of a matroid and uncertain clustering.
one_line_summary: Investigates local search methods for combinatorial multi-armed bandits to minimize online regret.
annotation: This paper studies combinatorial multi-armed bandits, a core online decision-making framework in AI/ML, by extending offline local search algorithms to the online stochastic setting. The central contribution is theoretical: deriving regret guarantees for local search methods analogous to those previously established for greedy and linear optimization approaches. This advances the algorithmic foundations of bandit learning, a primary topic in the machine learning and sequential decision-making literature.

title: RoguePrompt: Dual-Layer Encoding for Self-Reconstruction to Circumvent LLM Moderation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly integrated into mainstream development platforms and daily technological workflows, typically behind moderation and safety controls. Despite these controls, preventing prompt-based policy evasion remains challenging, and adversaries continue to "jailbreak" LLMs by crafting prompts that circumvent implemented safety mechanisms. Prior work has established cipher-mediated interaction, code-embedded decryption, prompt decomposition and reconstruction, and layered custom encryption as viable attack primitives. However, reported evaluations generally collapse visible acceptance, successful recovery of the concealed request, and subsequent execution into an aggregate attack-success outcome. This leaves limited evidence about where multistage prompt-transformation attacks fail within an observable black-box interaction. This paper introduces RoguePrompt, a jailbreak pipeline that partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested encodings, Vigenere followed by ROT13, along with natural-language reconstruction instructions. RoguePrompt was developed and evaluated under a black-box threat model, with only API or user-interface access to the hosted models, and was tested on 313 real-world, hard-rejected prompts. Success was measured in terms of moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution when the relevant stage exceeded its automated criterion. RoguePrompt achieved average rates of 93.93% for filter bypass, 79.02% for reconstruction, and 70.18% for execution. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of layered prompt encoding while providing stage-level evidence of where multistage jailbreaks fail during moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution.
one_line_summary: A dual-layer encoding attack method that circumvents LLM safety moderation through self-reconstruction prompts.
annotation: This paper introduces RoguePrompt, a jailbreaking technique that uses dual-layer encoding and self-reconstruction to evade LLM safety moderation systems. The work critically examines prior attack primitives—including cipher-mediated interaction, code-embedded decryption, and layered encryption—and identifies methodological gaps in how attack success is measured across multistage pipelines. By disaggregating acceptance, request recovery, and execution into distinct evaluation stages, the paper contributes both a novel attack method and a more rigorous framework for assessing LLM safety vulnerabilities.

title: Structured AI Demonstrations and Student LLM Use in Engineering Mechanics: Study Design and Preliminary Results
abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into undergraduate education presents an urgent challenge for engineering instructors. Despite widespread student adoption, there remains a critical lack of domain-specific empirical evidence to guide pedagogical policies and classroom interventions. This manuscript presents a descriptive study design and preliminary findings from an undergraduate engineering mechanics course conducted in Spring 2026. We detail a reproducible survey instrument used to capture student AI usage patterns, attitudes, and verification practices, which are subsequently linked to academic performance metrics. Additionally, we document a deployable sequence of nine structured, instructor-led AI demonstrations designed to model strategic LLM delegation and evaluation. While our preliminary data highlight shifting student behaviors and complex relationships between AI reliance and course outcomes, the primary contribution of this work is the provision of an open-access methodological framework. By making our complete study design, survey tools, and demonstration materials publicly available, we urge other engineering educators to collect and share similar empirical data. Navigating this unprecedented technological shift will require a collaborative, evidence-based approach to fully understand its long-term impacts on student learning.
one_line_summary: Study examining LLM use patterns and structured AI demonstrations in undergraduate engineering mechanics courses.
annotation: This paper investigates how undergraduate engineering students use large language models in an engineering mechanics course, documenting usage patterns, attitudes, and verification practices linked to academic performance. The study introduces a structured sequence of instructor-led AI demonstrations intended to model strategic LLM delegation. While LLMs are the subject of study, the paper does not build or evaluate AI systems but rather examines pedagogical approaches to AI integration in engineering education.

title: Taxonomy-Driven Analysis of Open-Source AI Risk Mitigation Tools
abstract: Rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in enterprise settings has introduced operational, security, and governance risks. As generative AI applications move from pilot to production, manual harm identification and mitigation are becoming difficult to scale. Although many tools support model evaluation, adversarial testing, runtime guardrails, and observability, the tooling landscape remains fragmented. Tools are typically designed for specific engineering tasks and described in technical terms that do not align with governance frameworks or risk taxonomies, making it difficult to determine which tools address which risks and where critical gaps remain. This paper proposes a structured protocol to automate AI risk mitigation through a taxonomy-driven analysis of open-source LLM evaluation and security tools. We map the capabilities of 21 prominent open-source tools to the 32 subcategories of the extended MIT AI Risk Mitigation and Response Taxonomy. An LLM-assisted retrieval-augmented generation pipeline analyzes source code and documentation to extract capabilities for each taxonomy category. Reliability assessment yielded moderate agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.509) among three independent reviewers. The analysis reveals a highly skewed landscape in which tools cluster around technical and operational controls, while governance, legal and regulatory, and financial and market controls remain largely unaddressed. This motivates a layered risk-mitigation architecture combining tool-based controls with organizational and regulatory processes. The mapping protocol achieved an F1 score of 75.5% after majority voting. Overall, the study provides a practical mapping between enterprise AI risk categories and open-source mitigation capabilities, identifies where human oversight remains necessary, and presents a taxonomy-driven framework applicable to open-source and proprietary solutions.
one_line_summary: A taxonomy-driven protocol for systematically analyzing open-source tools that mitigate LLM risks in enterprise settings.
annotation: This paper addresses the fragmented landscape of open-source tools for mitigating risks associated with large language models in enterprise deployments, including operational, security, and governance risks. It proposes a structured, taxonomy-driven protocol to systematically map evaluation, adversarial testing, guardrail, and observability tools to established risk frameworks, enabling automated harm identification at scale. The contribution is primarily in AI governance and safety, bridging the gap between technical tooling and governance taxonomies to identify coverage gaps in LLM risk mitigation.

title: Polarization in Quantum Optics: A new Formalism and Two Experiments
abstract: We report on two quantum polarization experiments. The first one shows that three geometrical rotations can in principle be distinguished with certainty using two photons. The second experiment shows quantum polarization properties of classically unpolarized light. We outline a new treatment of polarization in quantum optics. Our formalism differs from the usual quantum description, which uses the Stokes operators. These keywords were added by machine and not by the authors. annotation: This paper addresses online feedback optimization for stochastic problems where the underlying probability distribution depends on the decision variables, a setting relevant to performative prediction and adaptive control. The work develops algorithms that handle constraints while operating in an online fashion without full knowledge of the distribution. The contribution is primarily algorithmic, advancing optimization methodology applicable to learning systems and control engineering.

title: From predictive maintenance to prescriptive: A survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation-Driven Systems for End-to-End Maintenance Decision-Making
one_line_summary: Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems for end-to-end maintenance decision-making.
annotation: This survey examines the application of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems to industrial maintenance, tracing the evolution from predictive to prescriptive maintenance paradigms. The paper reviews how RAG-driven AI architectures integrate large language models with domain-specific knowledge retrieval to support end-to-end maintenance decision-making. As a comprehensive survey of AI methods and architectures applied to a specific engineering domain, it constitutes a primary AI contribution focused on the design and evaluation of RAG-based systems.

title: Who Welcomes AI? Individual and Cross-National Correlates of AI Optimism in 21 Countries
one_line_summary: Cross-national study of individual and country-level factors predicting AI optimism across 21 countries.
annotation: This paper investigates the individual and cross-national correlates of optimism toward artificial intelligence across 21 countries, examining how demographic, cultural, and institutional factors shape public attitudes. The study does not build or apply AI/ML models but instead uses survey data and statistical analysis to understand societal reception of AI technologies. It contributes to the growing literature on public opinion and AI governance by identifying who is most likely to welcome AI and why.

title: TriEval: A Resource-Efficient Pipeline for LLM Bias, Toxicity, and Truthfulness Assessment
one_line_summary: A resource-efficient pipeline for evaluating bias, toxicity, and truthfulness in large language models.
annotation: TriEval proposes a unified evaluation pipeline designed to assess three critical safety dimensions—bias, toxicity, and truthfulness—in large language models (LLMs). The paper's core contribution is a resource-efficient methodology for benchmarking LLM behavior across these dimensions, addressing practical constraints in model evaluation. This work sits at the intersection of AI safety, fairness, and NLP, contributing directly to the growing field of responsible AI assessment.

title: Adaptive Antitrust Agency Enforcement and the Use of AI: Legal and Policy Implications
one_line_summary: Examines legal and policy implications of AI use in antitrust agency enforcement.
annotation: This paper analyzes how antitrust regulatory agencies might adaptively employ AI tools in their enforcement activities, focusing on the legal and policy dimensions of such adoption. The work does not build or evaluate AI models but instead examines the governance, regulatory, and jurisprudential implications of integrating AI into competition law enforcement. It contributes to scholarship on AI regulation and the institutional design of adaptive agency rulemaking in the context of emerging technologies.

title: The Frontline Exposure Gap: Evidence on AI Adoption in Retail and Service Occupations from Task-Level Usage Data
one_line_summary: Examines AI adoption patterns in retail and service occupations using task-level usage data.
annotation: This paper investigates the gap between AI exposure predictions and actual AI adoption among frontline retail and service workers, using task-level usage data as empirical evidence. The study contributes to labor economics and workforce policy by documenting how AI diffusion differs across occupational strata, particularly for lower-wage frontline workers. While AI is the central subject of inquiry, the paper does not build or evaluate AI systems but rather analyzes the socioeconomic patterns of AI adoption in the labor market.

title: Breaking the Memory Wall: A Survey of Key-Value (KV) Cache Compression for Efficient Large Language Model (LLM) Inference&nbsp;
one_line_summary: Survey of KV cache compression techniques to improve memory efficiency in large language model inference.
annotation: This survey comprehensively reviews key-value (KV) cache compression methods designed to address memory bottlenecks during large language model inference. The paper systematically categorizes and evaluates techniques such as token eviction, quantization, and architectural modifications that reduce the memory footprint of attention mechanisms in transformer-based LLMs. As a survey of core AI/ML optimization methods, it constitutes a primary contribution to the field of efficient deep learning systems.
